team-notes:
Route reads and writes from the client through a medium app service to a medium SQL database. A read returns the stored note; a write commits the new version in SQL before the response travels back to the client. The database is the persistence boundary.

The reference keeps the path short and uses the same store for reads and updates. It does not need a cache or load balancer for this authored workload. The medium profiles trade additional provisioned cost for capacity; adding more components would add cost and request hops. Assess the steady and burst scenarios to evaluate the resulting design.
url-shortener:
Send both operations through a medium app service. Resolve requests check the large cache first; a cache miss reads the mapping from medium SQL and fills the cache. Create requests go directly from the app to SQL, so the new mapping is stored before success is returned.

The app also has a synchronous invalidation connection to the cache for creation. Cached mappings expire after 60 seconds. Popular existing mappings can be served through the cache, while SQL remains the persistent source. This introduces cache capacity, expiry, and miss handling in exchange for avoiding repeated database reads. Evaluate the burst as well as steady traffic; cache hits alone are not proof that the requirements are met.
product-catalogue:
Route product reads from the client through the medium app service to the large cache. Cache misses read from medium SQL and fill the cache. Product updates travel directly from the app to SQL, followed by synchronous invalidation of the cached product before acknowledgement.

Synchronous invalidation is the key freshness choice: the 60-second cache TTL alone is longer than the authored freshness allowance. The SQL database retains the committed versions, and the cache serves repeated reads. This adds an invalidation dependency to the write path. Assess cold-cache and burst scenarios as well as steady traffic, because losing cached entries shifts read work back to the database.
photo-delivery:
Serve photo reads from the client through the large CDN. A miss fetches the immutable object from the small object store and fills the CDN; cached objects expire after 60 seconds. Uploads go directly from the client to object storage, where the payload is stored before acknowledgement.

Separate read and upload routes fit the supplied immutable-photo operations. The CDN can serve repeated object bytes while object storage remains the persistent origin. The reference avoids routing large payloads through an app service. Inspect transfer capacity and the cold-CDN scenario as well as request count: a cold cache requires origin transfers, and the CDN adds provisioned cost.
notifications:
Send enqueue requests from the client through the small app service to the small message queue. The queue acknowledges accepted work, and a consume connection delivers jobs to a pool of six medium worker instances. Workers process jobs and record their effect in the simulation's recipient sink.

Acknowledgement and delivery are separate parts of the flow. Worker capacity must address the burst backlog as well as steady arrivals, within the authored job deadline and cost budget. Inspect first correct effects and duplicate effects alongside acknowledgement latency. The queue decouples acceptance from processing; an Accepted response by itself does not mean a notification was delivered.
first-design:
Connect Client → App → Database, selecting the read_note operation on both request connections. Use a small app service and change the database profile from small SQL to medium SQL. Keep a single instance of each component. A request enters the app, reads the note from SQL, then returns along the same path.

The database profile is the intended change from the starter. It provides more service capacity at a higher provisioned cost while keeping the architecture simple. Use Preview to inspect the request flow, then Assess design to evaluate all required checks. The resulting evidence, including successful read latency and cost, determines completion.
